contribution: Newton's second law $\Sigma\overline{F} = m\overline{a}$ is discovered from measurements on a cart: the acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass, and the net force points in the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity. The equation of motion is written only after the free-body diagram and the positive direction, in horizontal and vertical motion.
learn: explain how the acceleration depends on the net force and the mass.
work out the direction of the net force from the acceleration, also in slowing-down motion.
calculate an acceleration or a force using the free-body diagram and the equation of motion $\Sigma F = ma$.
prior: Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit of time, $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ (chapter *Acceleration and uniformly accelerated motion*)
When the forces acting on an object cancel each other, the object is at rest or moves at constant velocity (chapter *Interaction and force: Newton's first and third laws*)

activities.text: Two identical timber trucks stand side by side at the traffic lights. One is empty, the other is full of logs. The light turns green, and both drivers accelerate with equal effort. Within a few seconds the empty truck is clearly ahead.
activities.question: What decides how quickly the velocity of an object changes, and why does the same engine not get the loaded truck up to speed as quickly?

activities.title: Recall: uniform motion
activities.prompt: A puck slides straight ahead at constant velocity on horizontal ice. Friction and air resistance are so small that they are ignored. Which forces act on the puck?

choices.text: The weight and the normal force from the ice. They cancel each other, so the net force is zero.
choices.feedback: Correct. Only the Earth and the ice act on the puck. In the chapter *Interaction and force: Newton's first and third laws* you learned that uniform motion needs no forward force: when the net force is zero, the velocity stays the same.

choices.text: The weight, the normal force from the ice and a forward force that keeps the puck moving.
choices.feedback: Nothing pushes the puck while it slides, so there is no forward force. The puck keeps moving without a force, because the velocity changes only when the net force is not zero.

choices.text: Only the weight. The ice does not act on a moving puck.
choices.feedback: The puck does not sink through the ice, so the ice supports it upward. If nothing cancelled the weight, the puck would accelerate downward.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the force doubles
activities.prompt: A cart starts from rest on a horizontal track where friction is very small. A string pulls it with a constant force. What happens to the motion of the cart when the pulling force is doubled and the mass stays the same?

choices.text: The acceleration doubles: the velocity grows twice as much every second.
choices.feedback: Correct. In the values of the model, the acceleration of a $1.0\,\text{kg}$ cart is $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $1.0\,\text{N}$ and $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $2.0\,\text{N}$. The acceleration is directly proportional to the net force.

choices.text: The cart reaches twice the velocity and then continues steadily.
choices.feedback: A constant force does not give a constant velocity. In the graph the velocity keeps growing steadily and does not settle at any value. A force changes the velocity: a doubled force doubles the acceleration, in the values of the model from $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ to $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$.

choices.text: The acceleration does not change, because it depends only on the mass of the cart.
choices.feedback: The mass affects the acceleration, but so does the force. In the values of the model the same $1.0\,\text{kg}$ cart accelerates at $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $1.0\,\text{N}$ and at $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $2.0\,\text{N}$.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the mass doubles
activities.prompt: A string pulls a cart from rest with a constant force of $1.0\,\text{N}$. Weights are added to the cart so that its mass doubles. What happens to the acceleration?

choices.feedback: Correct. In the values of the model, the acceleration is $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a mass of $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a mass of $1.0\,\text{kg}$. The same force changes the velocity of an object with twice the mass half as fast.

choices.text: The acceleration stays the same, because the pulling force is the same.
choices.feedback: The force is the same, but it has to change the velocity of a greater mass. In the values of the model the acceleration drops from $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ to $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ when the mass grows from $0.50\,\text{kg}$ to $1.0\,\text{kg}$.

choices.text: The cart does not start moving if the pulling force is smaller than the weight of the cart.
choices.feedback: On a horizontal track the weight is vertical, and the normal force from the track cancels it. A horizontal pull does not have to overcome the weight: even $1.0\,\text{N}$ accelerates a cart whose weight is almost $10\,\text{N}$. In the values of the model the acceleration is then $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$.

activities.title: Prediction 3: a force against the motion
activities.prompt: A cart moves to the right. A string starts to pull it to the left with a constant force. In which direction does the acceleration of the cart point while the cart is still moving to the right?

choices.text: To the left, in the direction of the force: the cart slows down, stops for a moment and starts moving to the left.
choices.feedback: Correct. In the graph the velocity decreases steadily to zero and becomes negative with the same slope. In the values of the model the acceleration is $-2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ throughout the run, when $2.0\,\text{N}$ pulls a $1.0\,\text{kg}$ cart to the left.

choices.text: To the right, in the direction of motion, until the cart stops.
choices.feedback: The acceleration does not point in the direction of motion but in the direction of the change in velocity. The velocity of the cart to the right decreases, so the change points to the left. In the values of the model the acceleration is $-2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ even before the stop.

choices.text: The acceleration is zero until the cart stops, and then points to the left.
choices.feedback: If the acceleration were zero, the velocity would not change and the cart would not stop. In the graph the velocity decreases as soon as the string starts to pull. In the values of the model the acceleration is $-2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ all the time.

activities.text: In the simulation a string pulls a laboratory cart on a horizontal track. At the top is the situation picture, on the right the free-body diagram of the cart and at the bottom the velocity graph, whose slope is the acceleration.
activities.howto: Adjust the pulling force $F$ and the mass $m$. Choose whether the cart is at rest or moving to the right at the start, and which way the string pulls. Press *Start*. The run lasts $1.0\,\text{s}$ or ends before the end of the track. After the run an orange straight line is drawn in the graph, and its slope $a_x$ is shown in the readouts. *Reset* returns the cart to the start. *Speed* slows down or speeds up the motion without changing the readouts.
activities.model: The values are model values calculated by the simulation. The track is horizontal, and friction and air resistance are not taken into account. The weight $\overline{G}$, the normal force $\overline{N}$ from the track and the force $\overline{F}$ of the string act on the cart. The weight and the normal force cancel each other, so the net force is the force of the string. The force of the string stays constant throughout the run. The arrows in the free-body diagram are on one scale, so the pulling force looks short next to the weight.
activities.calc: The positive direction is to the right. The velocity $v_x$ of the cart is recorded in the graph every $0.05\,\text{s}$. The acceleration $a_x$ is the slope $\dfrac{\Delta v_x}{\Delta t}$ of the straight line fitted to the points. In the readouts $\Sigma F_x$ is the force of the string with its sign and $G = mg$, where $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the pulling force changes
activities.intro: Test the first prediction. The starting state selects a mass of $1.0\,\text{kg}$ and a cart at rest, and the string pulls to the right. Change only the force $F$. Press *Start* each time and record the measurement when the run has ended. Try at least the forces $1.0\,\text{N}$ and $2.0\,\text{N}$.

activities.title: Experiment 2: the mass changes
activities.intro: Test the second prediction. The starting state selects a force of $1.0\,\text{N}$ and a cart at rest, and the string pulls to the right. Change only the mass $m$. Press *Start* and record a measurement for each mass.

activities.title: Experiment 3: a force against the motion
activities.intro: Test the third prediction. The starting state selects a force of $2.0\,\text{N}$, a mass of $1.0\,\text{kg}$ and a cart that moves to the right at the start. Change only the direction of the string. During the run, watch the blue and the orange arrow and the points of the graph. Record a measurement for both directions.

question.prompt: When the string pulls to the left, the velocity of the cart is positive at the start and the acceleration is negative. What can be concluded from this?

choices.text: The net force and the acceleration point in the same direction, even though the velocity does not.
choices.feedback: Correct. In the table $\Sigma F_x$ and $a_x$ always have the same sign. The direction of the velocity does not decide the direction of the acceleration.

choices.text: The acceleration always points against the velocity when some force acts on the cart.
choices.feedback: When the string pulls to the right, the acceleration and the velocity are both positive. The acceleration follows the net force, not the velocity.

choices.text: The cart moves to the right at the start, so the net force also points to the right then.
choices.feedback: In the table $\Sigma F_x$ is negative throughout the run: the only horizontal force is the pull of the string to the left. The direction of motion does not produce a force.

activities.title: Conclusion
activities.prompt: Using your measurements, explain how the acceleration of the cart depends on the net force and the mass. Then explain why a loaded truck accelerates more slowly than an empty one when the force of the road on the tyres is the same.
criteria: The answer says that the acceleration doubles when the net force doubles and the mass stays the same.
The answer says that the acceleration is halved when the mass doubles and the force stays the same.
The answer uses your own measurement results, for example two accelerations and their ratio.
The answer explains the slower acceleration of the truck by its greater mass and not by the weight, which the normal force from the road cancels.
activities.model: In experiment 1 the mass was $1.0\,\text{kg}$. In the values of the model the acceleration was $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $1.0\,\text{N}$ and $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a force of $2.0\,\text{N}$: a doubled net force gave a doubled acceleration. In experiment 2 the force was $1.0\,\text{N}$. The acceleration was $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a mass of $0.50\,\text{kg}$ and $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ with a mass of $1.0\,\text{kg}$: a doubled mass halved the acceleration. So the acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass, $a = \dfrac{\Sigma F}{m}$. The mass of a loaded truck is many times that of an empty one. When the force of the road on the tyres is the same, the acceleration is that many times smaller. The weight of the load does not pull the truck backward, because the normal force from the road cancels it.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the measurements. What surprised you most? Write in your own words what the direction of the net force tells you and what it does not tell you.

activities.title: Choose the correct free-body diagram
activities.prompt: A crane lowers a crate downward on a rope. Just before the ground the crate slows down and stops. In which diagram is the free-body diagram of the crate correct during the slowing down? Air resistance is ignored. Each wrong diagram has one mistake.

choices.feedback: Correct. The crate moves down but slows down, so its acceleration points up. The net force must point in the direction of the acceleration: $T - G = ma$, so $T > G$.

Arrows of equal length mean that the net force is zero. The crate would then move at constant velocity and would not slow down. The acceleration of a slowing crate points up, so the force of the rope must be greater than the weight.

Here the net force points down, in the direction of the velocity. The velocity of the crate would then increase. During the slowing down the acceleration and the net force point up, against the motion.
Motion does not cause a force. The force $\overline{F}$ has no cause: only the Earth and the rope act on the crate. Otherwise the diagram would be correct.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A passenger car of mass $1400\,\text{kg}$ is driving on a horizontal road at a velocity of $72\,\text{km/h}$. The driver brakes, and the car stops, slowing down uniformly, in $4.0\,\text{s}$. What is the net force acting on the car during the braking? Give the answer in newtons.
hints: The net force is obtained from the law $\Sigma F = ma$. What do you need to know first, and where do you get it?
The acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$. First convert the velocity to $\text{m/s}$.

mistakes.feedback: You used the velocity $72$ as it was. The velocity must be converted to $\text{m/s}$ before the acceleration is calculated: $72\,\text{km/h} = 72 : 3.6\,\text{m/s} = 20\,\text{m/s}$.
This is the deceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$. The net force is obtained by multiplying it by the mass of the car: $\Sigma F = ma$.
This is the weight $mg$ of the car. The weight and the normal force from the road cancel each other, and they do not stop the car. The net force is horizontal: $ma$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 1400\,\text{kg}$, initial velocity $v_0 = 72\,\text{km/h}$, final velocity $v = 0$, time $\Delta t = 4.0\,\text{s}$, the car slows down uniformly

**Find:** the magnitude of the net force $\Sigma F$ in $\text{N}$

**Principle:** The velocity of the car changes steadily, so its acceleration is constant. By Newton's second law the net force is the mass times the acceleration, and it points in the direction of the acceleration, that is backward.

**Free-body diagram:** The car as a rectangle, the positive direction the direction of motion. The weight $\overline{G}$ points down from the centre and the normal force $\overline{N}$ from the road points up from the tyres, equally long. The friction force $\overline{F}_\mu$ from the road points backward from the contact point of the tyres. There is no force pushing forward.

**Formula:** $a = \dfrac{v - v_0}{\Delta t}$ and $\Sigma F = ma$, so $\Sigma F = \dfrac{m(v - v_0)}{\Delta t}$

**Conversions:** $72\,\text{km/h} = 72 : 3.6\,\text{m/s} = 20\,\text{m/s}$

**Substitution:** $\Sigma F = \dfrac{1400\,\text{kg}\cdot(0 - 20\,\text{m/s})}{4.0\,\text{s}} = 1400\,\text{kg}\cdot(-5.0\,\text{m/s}^2) = -7000\,\text{N}$

**Answer:** $7000\,\text{N}$ or $7.0\,\text{kN}$ backward, two significant figures like the time $4.0\,\text{s}$ and the velocity $72\,\text{km/h}$. The minus sign tells us that the force points against the motion.

**Reasonableness:** The weight of the car is about $14\,\text{kN}$, so the braking force is about half of the weight. The deceleration $5.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ is about half of the free-fall acceleration, which is an ordinary firm braking on a dry road. The force points backward even though the car moves forward, because the car is slowing down.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. When a task has forces, first draw the free-body diagram and choose a positive direction, and only then write $\Sigma F = ma$. Level 1 is enough for basic competence; levels 2 and 3 take it deeper.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: A ball has been thrown straight up, and it is still rising. Air resistance is ignored. Which statement about the net force on the ball is correct during the rise?

choices.text: The net force is the weight of the ball, and it points down even though the ball moves up.
choices.feedback: Correct. Once the thrower's hand has let go of the ball, only the Earth acts on it. The net force points down, so the acceleration also points down and the rising ball slows down.

choices.text: The net force points up, because the ball moves up.
choices.feedback: Motion does not cause a force. The force of the thrower acted only during the throw. During the rise only the weight acts on the ball, downward, and that is why the ball slows down.

choices.text: The net force is zero, because the force of the throw and the weight are equal.
choices.feedback: If the net force were zero, the ball would continue upward at constant velocity and would never turn back. There is no force of the throw any more once the hand has let go of the ball.

activities.title: 2. Calculation
activities.prompt: A shopping trolley of mass $18\,\text{kg}$ is pushed on a horizontal floor with a force of $30\,\text{N}$. The rolling resistance of the wheels and other friction slow the trolley with a total force of $12\,\text{N}$. What is the acceleration of the trolley? Give the answer in $\text{m/s}^2$.
hints: Draw the free-body diagram of the trolley. Which forces are horizontal, and which cancel each other in the vertical direction?
Choose the direction of the push as the positive direction. In the horizontal direction $F - F_\mu = ma$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided only the pushing force by the mass. The acceleration is determined by the net force, so first subtract the slowing $12\,\text{N}$: $\Sigma F = 30\,\text{N} - 12\,\text{N}$.
You added the forces together. The slowing force points against the push, so its sign is negative: $\Sigma F = 30\,\text{N} - 12\,\text{N} = 18\,\text{N}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $m = 18\,\text{kg}$, pushing force $F = 30\,\text{N}$ horizontally, slowing forces in total $F_\mu = 12\,\text{N}$

**Find:** the acceleration $a$ of the trolley in $\text{m/s}^2$

**Principle:** By Newton's second law the acceleration of the trolley is determined by the net force. In the vertical direction the trolley does not accelerate, so only the horizontal forces remain in the net force.

**Free-body diagram:** The trolley as a rectangle, the positive direction the direction of the push. The weight $\overline{G}$ points down from the centre and the normal force $\overline{N}$ from the floor points up from the bottom surface, equally long. The pushing force $\overline{F}$ points forward and the slowing force $\overline{F}_\mu$ points backward from the edge of the bottom surface, shorter than the pushing force.

**Formula:** $F - F_\mu = ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F - F_\mu}{m}$

**Conversions:** All quantities are in SI units, and $\tfrac{\text{N}}{\text{kg}} = \tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}$, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $a = \dfrac{30\,\text{N} - 12\,\text{N}}{18\,\text{kg}} = \dfrac{18\,\text{N}}{18\,\text{kg}} = 1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$

**Answer:** $1.0\,\text{m/s}^2$ in the direction of the push, two significant figures like the data $30\,\text{N}$, $12\,\text{N}$ and $18\,\text{kg}$.

**Reasonableness:** Without the slowing forces the acceleration would be $30\,\text{N} : 18\,\text{kg} \approx 1.7\,\text{m/s}^2$, so friction makes it smaller, as it should. An acceleration of $1\,\text{m/s}^2$ means that the velocity of the trolley increases by $1\,\text{m/s}$ every second, which fits a brisk push.

activities.title: 3. Draw it yourself
activities.prompt: A book of mass $1.2\,\text{kg}$ lies on a horizontal table. You push it horizontally with your hand with a force of $5.0\,\text{N}$, and the friction force from the table on the book is $3.0\,\text{N}$. Draw the free-body diagram of the book on paper: the book as a rectangle and every force from its point of action. Mark the direction of the acceleration separately next to the diagram. Then write the equations of motion in the horizontal and vertical directions and calculate the acceleration of the book.

criteria.detail: The diagram has only the book, no hand and no table with its own forces.
Four forces: the weight, the normal force from the table, the pushing force of the hand and the friction force from the table. No extra force in the direction of motion.
The weight down, the normal force up, the pushing force in the direction of motion and the friction against it.

The weight from the centre, the normal force from the bottom surface apart from the weight, the friction from the edge of the bottom surface outward from the book, the pushing force from the side of the book; each with its own symbol.
The normal force and the weight are equally long, the friction is shorter than the pushing force. The acceleration is marked separately and not as a force.
In the horizontal direction $F - F_\mu = ma$ and in the vertical direction $N - mg = 0$, the positive directions named; $a \approx 1.7\,\text{m/s}^2$.

activities.model: The Earth (weight $\overline{G}$), the table (normal force $\overline{N}$ and friction force $\overline{F}_\mu$) and the hand (pushing force $\overline{F}$) act on the book. In the vertical direction the book does not accelerate, so $N - mg = 0$ and $N = mg = 1.2\,\text{kg}\cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \approx 11.8\,\text{N}$. In the horizontal direction, when the positive direction is the direction of the push, $F - F_\mu = ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F - F_\mu}{m} = \dfrac{5.0\,\text{N} - 3.0\,\text{N}}{1.2\,\text{kg}} \approx 1.7\,\text{m/s}^2$. The net force $2.0\,\text{N}$ and the acceleration point in the direction of the push.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first by yourself and open the answer only afterwards.
